absent: Internal layout of tracepoint, module and tp_module structures and registration mechanics beyond enumeration.
Exact numeric values and bit positions for unwind control bits and full lifecycle of global availability mask and callback list beyond the cancel path.
Architecture-specific user frame layouts, register accessors and word-size determination for unwinding.
Perf event attribute structure, hardlockup panic flag definition and scheduler extension hook behavior referenced in the hardlockup path.
Softlockup timer handler, touch and report timestamp update rules and CPU utilization computation beyond stored state.
Watchdog mutex acquisition sites, CPU mask initialization and pending threshold application.
Sysfs attribute permissions and error handling for count files beyond successful registration.

findings.text: Two enumeration services exist for tracepoints. One walks every loadable module entry and invokes a caller callback with the tracepoint, its owner and a private token. The other walks the built-in kernel range delimited by linker symbols and invokes a simpler callback without module context.

Module tracepoint enumeration holds a dedicated list mutex for the whole walk, preventing concurrent mutation of the module collection while per-module iteration proceeds. Built-in range enumeration needs no such protection in the shown code.

Syscall tracepoint enablement follows a global reference count starting at zero. The first acquisition applies a syscall work flag to every thread in the system, and the last release clears that flag everywhere. Intermediate acquisitions and releases only adjust the count.

Transitions that touch all threads acquire the task list in shared mode while iterating over processes and threads, ensuring a stable thread set during flag updates. Count-only transitions take no lock.

Deferred unwind cache capacity is defined as the number of machine words that fit in a single 4K page after reserving space for the cache header. This bound sizes both allocation and unwind collection.

Two control signals named UNWIND_PENDING and UNWIND_USED are reserved. The global availability mask starts with exactly those signals set, while per-task masks start clear and later mix request bits with the same signals.
Whether deferred unwinding may run in nonmaskable interrupt context is a build-time choice with value one allowing such use and value zero forbidding it.

A dedicated mutex serializes mutation of the deferred unwind callback collection. Lifetime changes and cancellation hold it while unlinking entries and updating global availability, while invocation walks under a separate read-side mechanism.
Pending work is reported by testing a single bit in a per-task atomic mask. A set state means deferred processing has been requested and not yet collected.
A per-CPU 32-bit counter tracks unwind entry context nesting for the deferred mechanism. It is storage only in the shown fragments, with update rules defined elsewhere.

A fault-capable unwind service returns a cached user stack trace for the current thread. It requires an address space, allocates a page-sized entry cache on first use, reuses prior results within the same entry context, otherwise collects fresh frames up to the defined capacity and marks the cache as consumed for later cleanup on return to user mode. Missing address space and allocation failure are reported as distinct errors.

A direct user unwind routine fills a caller-provided trace with instruction addresses by walking frames until exhaustion or a caller limit. Zero limits are rejected, kernel threads yield an empty trace, and otherwise collection stops at the limit.

Deferred delivery clears the pending request atomically while retaining the set of requested callbacks, then obtains a trace that may legitimately be empty. Already completed requests are filtered using per-entry completion state, a stable task cookie is captured, and each remaining requested callback is invoked once and marked complete. The routine warns if entered without a pending request.

Deferred unwind work is scheduled through the generic task work facility and through a task exit hook. The work handler processes the current thread unconditionally, while the exit path processes only when work is pending and then withdraws the queued item.

Cancellation tolerates a null handle and rejects handles that use reserved control bits. Valid cancellation unlinks the entry under mutex, disables further requests by invalidating its slot, removes it from global availability, waits for in-flight readers, then clears the slot from every thread mask and from cached completion state.
Per-task unwind state starts zeroed with an initialized work item and a cleared atomic mask. Teardown releases the entry cache if present and withdraws any queued work item.

User stack walking validates each step before advancing. It derives a canonical address from frame or stack pointers plus an offset, requires forward progress and word alignment, reads return and frame values from user memory with 32-bit compatibility handling, and updates position accordingly. Entry state comes from current register values with kernel-thread and non-user rejection, frame-pointer support enabled only when built in, and iteration tries available methods in bit order until one succeeds or the walk ends.

Core watchdog tuning uses a sampling depth of five periods, a default threshold of ten, user master switches defaulting to enabled, a pending threshold holder, an availability flag, a global enable word, and a CPU membership mask with direct access to its underlying bits. Frequently read values are placed for read-mostly sharing.

Hard and soft lockup reporting expose separate all-CPU backtrace controls, system-info masks, miss tolerance defaulting to one, a soft panic flag defaulting from build configuration, an initialization marker, a sampling period, and a sentinel for delayed soft reports using the maximum unsigned long value.

Hard and soft lockup occurrences are each counted in a static unsigned accumulator exposed through a read-only sysfs file that prints the decimal value. Early initialization registers each file under the kernel object.

Boot-time strings control watchdog behavior. One disables the whole detector, another disables only soft detection, another sets the numeric threshold, and separate panic controls accept numeric input or comma-separated options where panic enables the panic path and nopanic disables it with zero and one as numeric toggles and a leading letter introducing raw perf configuration parsed as hexadecimal. A dedicated early hook can also turn off hard detection.

Hardlockup progress uses per-CPU interrupt counters with saved snapshots, missed counts, warned and touched flags, plus a global serialization word. Softlockup uses per-CPU touch and report timestamps, a high-resolution timer, a touch synchronization flag, and a separate global warning word. Touching is a lightweight per-CPU store safe for constrained contexts.

Hardlockup detection compares the current per-CPU interrupt count against a saved snapshot. A change resets the missed tally, while stability increments it and only signals after reaching the configured miss tolerance. Explicit touches also reset state. The timer tick path increments the local count and delegates checking of a successor CPU selected by wrapping membership iteration, with an empty fallback when the mechanism is disabled.

The hardlockup report path is designed for nonmaskable contexts. It suppresses duplicate warnings per CPU, serializes all-CPU dumps with a single global bit, emits an emergency notice before acquiring print synchronization to avoid deadlock, then dumps modules and interrupt state with local register or stack details or triggers a remote backtrace, optionally fans out to remaining CPUs, emits additional system information, and panics when configured.

Hardlockup control hooks have weak defaults that do nothing or report absence of a device, allowing architecture code to override them. The composite enable word is recomputed from master and per-type user switches gated by availability, yielding distinct hard and soft enable signals.

Softlockup diagnostics sample CPU time distribution over a short history. A small group enumeration covers system and interrupt and idle categories with a count sentinel, a fixed table maps groups to kernel time counters, and per-CPU storage keeps prior snapshots, a ring of recent utilization bytes, and a tail index.
A dedicated watchdog mutex exists for serializing detector configuration changes. The protected fields and acquisition sites are not visible in the routed fragments.
The default for hardlockup user enablement is build-dependent with value one enabling and value zero disabling. Kernel messages from this file carry a common watchdog textual prefix.

User unwinding touches user memory and therefore requires a fault-capable context and must avoid nonmaskable contexts unless explicitly permitted by build configuration. Deferred delivery mitigates this by caching results per entry and deferring callbacks to task work or exit paths.
